speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether he would care to comment on the statement made at his press conference yesterday by the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom indicating strong support for an Atlantic free trade area.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REPORTED
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY U.K. PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the course of the discussions that took place between the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom and myself, one of the most important subjects discussed was trade, and in particular the United Kingdom's relationship with Europe. Mr. Macmillan explained at length the position of the United Kingdom in regard to trade, and naturally there was an expression of the need for the widest possible expansion of trade and the strengthening of the economic relations among the countries of the Atlantic community. It was recognized that this relationship which is developing in Europe is one that will take a very considerable period of time.
In so far as the United Kingdom's attitude toward the common market is concerned Mr. Macmillan left me with the clear impression that the United Kingdom government intends to make every effort to work out a satisfactory means of participating in the economic organization of Europe without in any way detrimentally affecting Canada's trade. This he envisages as a major step forward which ultimately may lead to a wider development of trade to encompass the Atlantic community.

speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. Can the Prime Minister say whether the government has received Bill No. 56 of the Saskatchewan legislature, which the lieutenant governor refused to sign? Has the governor in council given consideration to this bill, and when will the government have an announcement to make?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: RESERVATION OF LEGISLATION RESPECTING MINING CONTRACTS
speechtext:
I read in the press that the hon. gentleman has already made a lengthy statement in this connection without full regard for the constitutional procedure which must be followed.
The course taken is that which has usually been followed throughout the years since the days of Sir John A. Macdonald, with the possible exception of 1937, when the lieutenant governor of Alberta reserved assent for the consideration of the Governor General in regard to three pieces of legislation in that province. The reservations by lieutenant governors have been generally accepted as dependent upon a request from the governor in council. There was no discussion in this regard, as I have already pointed out. We had no knowledge of the action to be taken by the lieutenant governor. However, the action was taken, and as yet the reasons which the lieutenant governor is required to transmit to the Governor General for the course he followed have not come to hand. As soon as they do the governor in council will take such action as is deemed proper, with full regard to the fact that this government has consistently taken the attitude that if legislation is within the legislative competence of the provinces, except constitutionally in extraordinary circumstances there should be no interference with provincial jurisdiction.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on the point of order raised in regard to my responsibilities as a member of this house, I suggest that I have already fulfilled my responsibilities in making my position clear, and I suggest that the record will show that the Prime Minister by very definite inference has criticized the lieutenant governor of Saskatchewan.

subtopic: RESERVATION OF LEGISLATION RESPECTING MINING CONTRACTS
speechtext: So there will be no mistake about that, Mr. Speaker, I pointed out that the lieutenant governor had certain responsibilities under the constitution. I also pointed out the manner in which they had been discharged generally since the days of Sir John A. Macdonald. The power is there, and it is not for me to say whether or not at this time the government of Canada is in full accord or in accord at all with the attitude or action taken. I understand that recent negotiations with the government at Peking for the sale of Canadian grain, especially wheat, have been handicapped by the lack of adequate facilities for loading grain on the west coast. If newspaper reports can be relied upon, I believe even the minister admitted that the sales might have been larger had there been greater facilities for the loading of the ships.
For a considerable number of years now on the west coast we have been handicapped by the lack of adequate facilities for the loading of ships. I believe I am right in saying that Canadian grain producers have received less than they might have received if at all times there had been adequate loading facilities on the west coast. Many a shipment has had to go by way of the St. Lawrence route or maybe even the Hudson bay route which could have been more economically served out of west coast ports. However, because of the inadequacy of our facilities the grain had to be moved to Hudson bay or to the head of the lakes, or even indeed to Halifax or Saint John. The interest being shown in Asia in Canadian grain has aggravated the problem.
I know the minister was out in British Columbia rather recently and he realizes the

conditions that have prevailed. The minister pleaded for more facilities. Like the late Will Rogers, all I know is what I read in the papers, but I understand that the minister appealed to private enterprise to build the additional facilities that are so urgently-needed on the west coast. We have a wonderful harbour there on Burrard inlet, covering North Vancouver, North Burnaby and Port Moody; and there is all kinds of room there for the building of additional terminals and facilities for the loading of ships with Canadian grain. If we look ahead and begin to anticipate the movement that grain is likely to follow in years to come, I think we cannot blind our eyes-

World movements of grain are very indefinite. The patterns may radically alter. I think it is too much to expect private enterprise to interest itself at this 90205-6-227

stage when we cannot clearly look into the future, and to risk tens of millions of dollars in building new and adequate terminal facilities in the lower mainland of British Columbia.
I believe this is a case in which the government itself must take whatever risk is involved in building additional facilities. I believe the minister is most unrealistic when he expresses the hope that the private grain trade is going to risk the large amount of capital that is involved in this particular matter. I believe the government ought to recognize that in the next 30, 40, 50 or even 100 years the countries of Asia are going to be the major markets for Canadian grain. Private enterprise are not likely to risk this investment because they might have to operate at a deficit for five, ten or any number of years in the future, and in the national interest the government ought to consider that it is responsible for ensuring that at all times adequate receiving and loading facilities will be available on the west coast.
I recommend to the minister that he give up his vain wish that the private grain trade might build additional terminals on Burrard inlet, and I hope the government will give very serious consideration to building these new terminals. I should especially commend Burrard inlet and the city of Port Moody to the minister, and I would ask that no time be lost in this regard, because from the time of the conception of a terminal until its completion a number of years must necessarily elapse.
I hope the government will make up its mind that Asia offers a terrific potential in the way of markets for Canadian grain and that this grain can be most economically exported from the lower mainland of British Columbia. I suggest it is a vain hope to expect the private grain industry to build the necessary facilities, and I hope the government will realize its responsibility to the economy not only of the grain producers of the prairies but also of the lower mainland of British Columbia. I hope the government will take immediate steps to ensure that additional terminals and loading facilities are built as soon as possible on Burrard inlet, and especially within the limits of the city of Port Moody.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to say a few words in connection with this matter of grain storage and the facilities for their shipment from the port of Vancouver. I was rather surprised that this discussion arose at this time rather than under the estimates of the national harbours board, but as you have allowed a discussion on this matter perhaps it would be fitting that I should say a few words at this time.

Supply-Agriculture
I wish to only partially endorse the remarks of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. I say "only partially" because the hon. member has taken a situation and is trying to build it up for his own advantage and political use in the future, rather than facing the facts. The facts are that the present Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce, by virtue of an aggressive, positive approach to Asian markets, have today brought into sharp focus the need for additional facilities for grain storage and shipping which would not be apparent had not the government, the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce created, developed and encouraged these markets.
Having said a few words of appreciation of those who most deserve it, I do wish to endorse the remarks of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam in bringing forward the need for a general improvement and increase of grain storage facilities, not only in the port of Vancouver but in other logical situations on the lower mainland of British Columbia.
It is perhaps an odd thing for a member for Coast-Capilano to speak on the agriculture estimates. I can, I think, say that few members which have rural areas have less to do with agriculture directly than I have in my riding. However, when it comes to the question of the port of Vancouver and other outlets on the lower mainland of British Columbia, these are our affairs. I should like to urge upon the minister that consideration be given not only to the establishment of further terminal elevator facilities in the area of the port of Vancouver, but also to the establishment of such facilities in the area of Squamish at the upper end of Howe sound to serve the vast output of grain which now has to pass through the port of Vancouver via the Pacific Great Eastern railroad and on a very detrimental basis to the farmers of the Peace river bloc due to the switching and bridge charges which are incurred at the present time in the area of Burrard inlet and within the jurisdictional area of the port of Vancouver.
I should like to again thank the Minister of Agriculture for his wisdom and courage in drawing together the shipping fraternity of the west coast, representatives of agricultural groups and businessmen generally of the lower mainland of British Columbia. We who live around the port of Vancouver take great pride in that very important facility. We feel that as a national harbour it represents a national trust. We feel strongly that we have a responsibility to the farmers of the

whole of western Canada to see that adequate storage and loading facilities are available at all times.
The Minister of Agriculture has certainly performed a great service not only to the port of Vancouver but to grain shippers throughout western Canada in bringing into being the committee which is now studying this matter. I think perhaps the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam was a little in error in his remarks as I do not think the minister called directly on private enterprise to build terminal grain facilities. The practice in most ports of Canada for many years has been that the national harbours board constructs the facilities. These facilities are in turn leased on a long term basis to the line elevator companies and the various pool and marketing organizations which handle grain in bulk.
I hope and trust that the committee which is now studying terminal grain facility requirements on the west coast will come forward with basic, sound and positive recommendations. This would certainly marry in with the current study, which I believe has been reported to the Minister of Transport, on the development of port facilities in the general area of Burrard inlet.
In concluding my remarks I should like to again point out the great advantage which would be gained by the grain shippers in the Peace river bloc through the establishment of terminal facilities at the head of Howe sound along the Pacific Great Eastern railroad, thus relieving these grain growers of the inordinately high switching charges they now face in moving grain from Squamish to the port of Vancouver and around its complete perimeter.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the question that has been raised by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, which is now receiving some support from the hon. member for Coast-Capilano-

speechtext: I have put forward this suggestion for three years.

subtopic: INSTRUCTIONS TO CUSTOMS AND POLICE OFFICIALS
speechtext:
It is an exceedingly important one and action should be taken immediately to deal with it. For many years we have been told by government spokesmen that the reason farm markets have been low or inadequate was because of the lack of overseas markets, that nothing could be done about this or, alternatively, that the government was doing everything possible to achieve larger sales abroad. The fact of the matter is that markets can be obtained, but shipping facilities, storage facilities and harbour facilities are inadequate. I think that in addition to the minister's trip to Vancouver and British Columbia, for which we thank

him-we are pleased he made it-he should see that definite action is taken to increase storage and handling facilities.
The hon. member for Coast-Capilano says it is worth while raising the subject but that this is not the item on which to discuss it. I am not particularly concerned about the procedural wrangle. I think this is a proper place to discuss this matter because in my judgment storage facilities and terminal facilities would be forthcoming if there were a well-established policy on the part of the board of grain commissioners to license such additional storage.
I think the government of Canada has the funds necessary to provide additional terminal facilities at Vancouver and Prince Rupert as well as to improve the facilities along the St. Lawrence. The St. Lawrence seaway needs a lot of improvement; it has been a fairly drastic failure as far as the achievement of the forecasts made for it are concerned. The government surely has money for this job. But I tell the Minister of Agriculture that if the government is short of money all it needs to do is to make an announcement that additional terminal facilities are required, that the board of grain commissioners is prepared to license them, that markets are improving in respect of sales going through the Pacific ports, and then the producers themselves would put up the money. The grain producers on the prairies have already built the major facilities in the west. The Alberta wheat pool, the Saskatchewan wheat pool, the Manitoba wheat pool and the united grain growers have already done most of this job and if there is a question of a shortage of facilities, as the minister claims there is, and as other hon. members have stated to be the case, if the government does not wish to take the initiative and if the deficit is so great that no more money can be found, then give the grain producers and their organizations a chance and they will build the facilities so that these important markets for Canadian grain may be obtained.
On this item I should like to ask the minister whether there is any possibility of a change of policy on his part and on the part of the board of grain commissioners with regard to the licensing of off-site storage. Five or six years ago the late Right Hon. C. D. Howe together with the board of grain commissioners decided to license certain offsite storage which was not in the hands of the elevator companies. This storage was often owned by community organizations which had storage facilities built in the form of quonset huts, the type of building which could be converted into a skating rink, a 90205-6-227*
Supply-Agriculture
curling rink or a community centre, if, some day, it was no longer needed for storage purposes.
Those of us in this group supported that policy. We pointed out that as long as the farmers had to pay the storage and as long as the people of Canada had to pay the storage to a substantial degree through the federal treasury it was far better to bring into being community facilities which would assist communities than to line the already gold-plated pockets of the elevator companies of this country. Nothing, to my mind, is as nauseating and repugnant as to hear private grain companies extol the private enterprise system knowing full well that under the present congested conditions there is little competition and that all they have to do is sit at ease, cash the storage cheques and make a very lucrative profit without having to show initiative in obtaining purchases of grain in a competitive situation.

speechtext:
On the contrary the farm organizations are doing a tremendous job. They are the only people who are doing the job and they will not look very kindly on the hon. member or on any of his friends who are associated with him when he sets himself up to criticize the farm organizations after they have done such a marvellous job in this field. The complaint he has made is that the government has not done enough. Now he complains when we say that if the government wants to sit on its fanny the farmers themselves are prepared to do something if they are told it is the policy of the board of grain commissioners and the government to license these facilities and if the statement is made that those facilities are needed and will be used.
I was talking about off-site storage facilities on the prairies and I was expressing the hope that the government would revert to a policy which I think was an excellent one, worthy of being implemented again. In the provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba there is a great need for storage facilities at this time and I suggest to the minister that the board of grain commissioners should license such off-site storage immediately. I think the farmers of Manitoba should make a loud protest at the great discrimination which is being shown them under the present marketing system as far as their marketings are concerned. I am wondering whether the inability or the refusal of the government to take steps to give the farmers of Manitoba anywhere near the kind of marketing shake which is being received by the farmers of Alberta is because large parts of Manitoba are a deficit grain producing area and the government wants to keep the grain producers of Manitoba in the clutches of the feed mills where they now rest. I suggest that in Manitoba there is a need for off-site storage so that farmers can get out a larger quantity of grain.
In Manitoba as of April 3, 131 marketing points were on a one-bushel quota. Manitoba's crop year is two-thirds over, and out of the prospects of marketing-I would hope at least seven bushels-they have only one bushel marketed. The minister says everything is fine and the government is taking every possible step to market the farmers' grain but the Manitoba farmers are getting a dirty deal. They have 149 marketing points with a two-bushel quota.

When considering Saskatchewan's marketing position we find that the picture is a little brighter but not much. It is still dark and gloomy. I would like to have the maps that are in the possession of the minister showing the quotas at the various marketing points. I would venture to guess that the farmers in his constituency are among the worst off in his regard. I would venture to guess that the farmers in my own riding have received the same kind of shabby treatment as those farmers in the minister's riding. Out of a total of 1,077 marketing points in Saskatchewan no less than 499, as of April 3, were on a two-bushel quota. I know from practical experience that all of the two-bushel quota has been delivered, or the points would be increased. The majority of farmers in Saskatchewan, according to the statistics, have not had the opportunity of selling to date even a full two-bushel quota. I think this is a horrible situation. I think that in this situation the board of grain commissioners and the government should consider emergency action which would allow the farmers in Manitoba and Saskatchewan, and wherever else discrimination may exist, as in Alberta -there the picture is much brighter-to get the same kind of treatment as the farmers receive in more favourable positions.
We heard last fall about the terrible grain handlers' strike in Vancouver. The minister's main comment in this regard was, why doesn't Hazen Argue settle it? The minister did not do much to settle it. It is a very strange thing that although this strike-it was a very serious thing which I hope will not happen again-took place at Vancouver, the Alberta farmers were far better off than Manitoba farmers where there was no interference in marketing grain to the east. I do not think there can be any co-relation between a strike and the movement of grain. I cannot see any connection at all, and this would almost prove that the Manitoba farmers should have been doing the same thing to get themselves in the horrible position of the Alberta farmers who have done so well relatively in the marketing of their grain.
I would make the suggestion that off-site storage should once again be considered and provided. I am aware of a situation existing in a little village in Saskatchewan called Drinkwater. A few years ago the residents of Drinkwater built a quonset-type hut that serves as a rink and holds about 80,000 bushels of wheat. They had it licensed by the board of grain commissioners, and that is why it is in order for me to discuss it under this item. This community association, which owns the rink, receives storage payments. They have been doing well. That little

town is starting to build some community facilities. On Easter Monday night they had an opening function in the Drinkwater community hall which was built in part under the government winter works program. Let us give the government credit for that; $4,000 was provincial and federal government money representing work and wages. The rest of the cost was money derived from the late C. D. Howe's very short-lived program allowing off-site storage.
The people of Drinkwater own the quon-set hut, which is full of wheat, and are receiving revenue from the storage of the wheat. The wheat remains in good condition and will not rot as a lot of wheat used to in the old annexes that the elevator companies owned. These people now have a community hall and are very proud of it. The next community facility they are going to build is a curling rink. They thought they were building a curling rink when they put up this quonset hut, of which 1 speak, but they promptly filled it with wheat. They are now going to build a curling rink to be paid for out of revenue from the storage of wheat in the quonset hut.
I would suggest that it is much better to give this revenue to similar community associations rather than to the famous Canadian grain company, the Patterson company. I do not think we need increase the profits to the Patterson Grain Company, the McCabe Elevator Company, the Federal Grain Company or the National Grain Company, or even to the Ogilvie Flour Mills Company, because the late C. D. Howe sold that a few years ago. I think it is far better that the profits from the storage of grain, wherever possible, should go to benefit the local community instead of going to line the pockets of the already well-heeled elevator companies in this country.
I suggest as well that this would be a very good program and is a necessary one at this time. It would be an emergency program- I would hope of a more than temporary nature-to deal with this very serious situation regarding grain delivery quotas. At the majority of points in western Canada even today the quotas are one and two bushels per acre. I suggest that the board of grain commissioners, carrying out a policy that I hope will be enunciated by the minister, will license local storage off-site in the villages and on farms. I do not see why the elevator companies should have all the storage while the farmer who has to store the grain receives nothing for doing so. I would suggest offsite storage should be allowed in villages and on farms up to a delivery quota of eight bushels per specified acre. If this were done the farmers throughout the prairie provinces
Supp ly-A griculture
would have the same opportunity of receiving revenue from grain storage and would not have to face the discrimination that flows from the geography of the prairie provinces and from the fact that some of the producers are fortunate enough to live near to Vancouver while some are unfortunate, in a marketing sense, in living closer to the great lakes' terminal facilities.
I would like to see the minister and the government take steps to increase the flow of grain not only through western ports but through eastern ports, and I suggest in all seriousness that the board of grain commissioners should consider off-site storage, to be owned by communities and by farmers, and that this off-site storage should be allowed up to a quota of eight bushels per acre.
Some years ago we had a very long and bitter debate in this house on the question of cash advances for farm stored grain. As I remember we were debating bank loans at the time, and the attitude of the C.C.F. group at that time was that the bank loan legislation was inadequate and should therefore be opposed. This was debated day after day for a week. We continued to oppose the bank loan legislation even though the then leader of the opposition, the Hon. George Drew, had said that it was better than nothing and that his party would vote for it. After the week of debate the official opposition of that day, the Progressive Conservative party, changed its position and joined us in opposing, condemning and voting against- you might even say filibustering, although that is a bad word-the bank loan legislation. We made the bank loan legislation so repugnant to Canadian farmers and generated such a demand for cash advances, interest-free, that this government, when it achieved office, had no alternative but to bring in that kind of legislation, for which we give it credit. I am suggesting that we must have a campaign for off-site storage providing a guaranteed delivery or sale, I suggest up to eight bushels per specified acre. The minister may say that this is too high, but the principle should be established that where marketing facilities have not been available for a standard quota agreed to and announced in advance, that facilities will be provided and licensed by the board of grain commissioners to provide for the sale of grain on this basis. The grain can be purchased in the farmer's bin. The grain elevator agent can go out and look at the bin, measure it, test the grain, dock it and estimate the number of bushels. He will be exceedingly accurate because the agents are used to this and they are able to do that kind of thing.
I suggest that, having licensed the facilities, the Canadian wheat board could issue a cash

Supp ly-A griculture
ticket to the farmer for his grain up to the eight-bushel quota. This kind of legislation is necessary if the western grain producer is to get a fair deal. This must be part of the Magna Carta of the grain producers. I am suggesting that, under this item, the minister should tell us that the board of grain commissioners and the government are prepared to consider the licensing of off-site storage so that the farmers whom X represent will be able to deliver the good quality grain they have on their farms. I feel very strongly about this. I feel it is abhorrent that farmers in one part of the country should face financial hardship through no fault of their own because they are unable to deliver the good quality grain that they have on their farms owing to the inability of our grain handling and marketing facilities to take care of quotas on a more equitable and uniform basis.
No doubt the discussion of this item will take some time. I should like the minister to reply to this suggestion as soon as he can. In any event, before this item passes I hope the minister will be able to inform the committee that the government will once again consider off-site storage and will assure Western producers of being able to market their current crop, or a minimum quantity of grain, and that quotas will be equalized in the three prairie provinces and in the Peace river bloc of British Columbia.

any market in the world with the knowledge that our grades will be accepted. This government, from the very beginning, has sought to move grain and to utilize the facilities that are in existence. This has been one of the objectives toward which farmers and farm organizations have worked over a long period of years. (2) Subject to (1) above and as far as current circumstances and reasonable equality in delivery opportunity permits, it should be your objective to provide:

Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman. It is very difficult for one with just an ordinary voice to compete. I will abide by your ruling and stay on the question of the board of grain commissioners.
The board of grain commissioners has been brought under the Department of Agriculture because it is so closely associated with the handling of grain in western Canada. When the Canadian wheat board was put under the Department of Agriculture it was done for the good, solid reason of trying to put under the Department of Agriculture not only the scientific and production efforts of the government but also the marketing efforts of the government concerned with grain.
The board of grain commissioners is part of the marketing efforts of the government. It is the board's responsibility to maintain, not only the standards of grain sold at every grade but also the standards of handling the grain in the elevator and to see that the farmer's interests are protected in connection with the grading of wheat and every other type of grain operation in the country elevator system.
The reputation of the board of grain commissioners has developed over the years so that today we can go into any market in the world and say we have certain grades to sell and that grade will be accepted as the standard that will be delivered.
This problem of maintaining the standard is not easily held. The question of grading grain is something that has to be seen in order to be understood. I should like to invite every hon. member of the committee, from all parties, to make an effort some time this year to visit the operations of the board of grain commissioners in Winnipeg and see the methods they use in arriving at and maintaining grades at a constant level.
This would enable the rural members particularly to explain to their constituents not

Supp ly-Agriculture
only the protection which is afforded by maintaining these standards but also the high level of excellence which Canadian wheat has reached and which enables the Canadian wheat board to sell it abroad.
The second point I wish to make is that the board of grain commissioners have an important function in the movement of grain out of the country. When I looked into the situation concerning the movement of grain out of west coast ports I found that one of the important operations that went on there was the grading of grain as it went into the ships. I was told we could not increase the movement of grain through the terminal elevators into the ships because the board of grain commissioners had to carry out a certain amount of grading in connection with every bushel put into these ships.
We discussed this matter with the board of grain commissioners and worked out a system whereby if they wanted to load at night or after dark, certain types of daylight lamps could be used in order to maintain the very high standards necessary to guarantee the calibre of our grain to any of our customers. I am glad to have this opportunity to point out this one technical aspect of the work of the board of grain commissioners.
I cannot answer the question of the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek. speechtext: I should like to say a few words on item 33. Those of us who live in the prairie region of western Canada, who, by reason of the Easter recess had opportunity to pay one of our very infrequent trips to our own areas, came back to Ottawa with some grim forebodings.

I am not speaking politically. Let me say that if these hon. gentlemen in the opposition would occasionally, even very occasionally, shelve their politics and deal with the actualities of the problems in Canada, this house would gain in dignity

and they would render a great service to their own constituencies and to the country at large.
We came back to Ottawa with some forebodings. Those forebodings were engendered by the spectre of drought in western Canada. Up to about four years ago we had 10 years of better than average precipitation. We had no real water worries and yet for the last four years, in each year there has been less and less precipitation, and we find ourselves this spring in a position with no reserves of moisture and a very dark outlook with respect to the forthcoming crop, and, what may prove even worse a real problem with respect to grass.
As you well know, sir, we live in what has been described as the Palliser triangle. More than 100 years ago Palliser recommended that this particular area should never see the plow. Unfortunately, in the enthusiasm of settlement, it saw a good many plows and we cultivated areas which should have remained under grass. There is promise under this government's legislation of placing those areas back under grass. I for one heartily commend the minister in his endeavour to develop a long range program which will bring back to western Canada its own natural advantages. At the moment the great question in the minds of those of us who come from my area is this: Are we going back to the dustbowl conditions of the 30's? Are we going back to the policy-and I am not criticizing that policy-where, under government supervision, we were forced to sell our cattle for what we could get? In the 30's, the price was three cents a pound. We sold thousands of head in order to save them from starvation.
Since the war years we have built a tremendous cattle industry in western Canada. Let me say that this industry has been the bulwark of agriculture in much of western Canada. We talk a lot about wheat but cattle have been the prop under which agriculture has rested in western Canada, especially in so far as the semi-arid regions are concerned. I, for one, am greatly concerned as to what may happen to this industry if dustbowl conditions return and we have insufficient grass and water to carry our cattle through this season.
Let me say very briefly that our water supply is generated on the eastern slopes of the Rockies. The snowfall in recent years in that area has been very light, and it was very light again this year. Our rivers and streams are very low, and there is no indication of improvement unless there are heavy rains within the next two months. After that, it may be too late.

This is all a prelude, Mr. Chairman, to urging upon the minister the necessity for an immediate, dynamic program of water conservation. Again I congratulate him for what he has done. He has been in consultation with men resident in my area and in other adjacent areas. He has met many of the officers of the Western Canada Reclamation Association who long have been and are seized with the importance of this problem. I am quite sure he will make it a point to accept their advice and be guided, at least to a large extent, by their opinions.
This item also deals with further work on the South Saskatchewan river development. I have spoken on this subject before. It is a three-way development. It promises power, it promises a domestic water supply for the cities and towns, and it promises irrigation. Now, we in Alberta are not jealous of Saskatchewan in so far as the South Saskatchewan dam is concerned. However, we do urge that in the dispersal of federal funds, further consideration be given to the already existing irrigation districts in Alberta. My reason for advancing this suggestion is that most of these districts were developed by private corporations. My own district, the eastern irrigation district, was developed by the Canadian Pacific, as were others. The Canadian Pacific found it expensive to maintain. Finally, they went to the farmers in the district and said, "This load is too heavy for us; you take it over and we will give it to you. We will also give you $300,000 as an operating fund and you carry on from there." I am very proud of the manner in which our men have continued that operation. I have had the privilege of managing the district for a few years. Certainly, the farmers have made good.
A stage has been reached in this irrigation project where the main structure, the Bassano dam, is now beginning to go. This is one of the best dams in the world, but it is now 50 years old. There are many other structures, such as the aqueduct at Brooks-which many hon. members may have seen from the train- which is beginning to go. The people of the district and the province of Alberta have not the financial capacity to replace these structures. Last year the minister was very generous in connection with the construction of one project in which we were very interested. The government was very generous. Let me record the thanks to him of the people concerned for that help. Let me say to him that if we are to preserve our existing irrigation districts, we shall require further help. I ask him to see that we get it.

I should like to comment on water projects as they affect the constituency of Rosetown-Biggar in central Saskatchewan. First, the policy of water conservation with dugouts and dams has made a big improvement in Saskatchewan. As a young man I went west. I started farming in 1919 at 19 years of age. The first two crops were failures. We had the best of land, but drought caused two crop failures in succession. I did not get out of debt until 1923 and we had a few wet years.
We have wonderful land. A lot of it should not have been broken up, I admit. We have a long growing season and freedom from frost. But our worry was drought. Starting farming at the age I did, the thought uppermost in my mind was water conservation. When you see the fields all flooded in spring you cannot help regretting that the water will all run off into the river and eventually into lake Winnipeg. This conservation program of dams

and dugouts has improved our pasture land for stock and irrigation projects.
Speaking of the Saskatchewan river dam, I was down there last week. In fact, they wrote to me regarding conditions at that time. First, I visited the P.F.R.A. camp. If there is in Ottawa or elsewhere a cleaner and better place to eat than the P.F.R.A. camp I should like to see it. I had many meals there. The floors are polished every day. The P.F.R.A. staff are living two men to a room, some of them with bath and toilet facilities. I went from there to the Kewitt, Johnson and Poole camp. That is where I had my dinner that day. The kitchen and dining rooms were clean. There was a choice of T-bone steak with mushrooms or hamburger steaks with onions. They invited me in to see their bedrooms. The bedrooms were clean. I would not mind sleeping in any room that I went through that day.
I went through Pigott's contruction camp on the other side of the river and have had meals there. I do a lot of visiting in that area and accept meals whenever I can. The meals I received at the Pigott camp on the west side of the river were very wholesome. I was informed that the only thing the men were required to do was keep their rooms clean. I was asked to look at the rooms to see whether they were dirty, and must say that some did have dirt on the floors but others were cleaned up and had pin-up girls on the walls and I thought were very nice places to stay.
There was some complaint about a year ago in regard to wages paid at these camps. I made an investigation in this regard and found that labourers building the camps were paid at the rate of $1.25 per hour. Individuals working on bridge construction as labourers received $1.45 per hour, and steam engineers firing the boilers received $1.90 an hour. At Smith Brothers-Wilson Camp carpenters were receiving $1.90 per hour plus $100 per month maintenance allowance while away from home. There were 15 farm boys from the town of Hawarden working there receiving $1.75 an hour driving nails. They were not required to handle a saw because everything was pre-cut before it arrived at the job. I may say that the officers of the Kewitt, Johnson and Poole camp received a letter of apology from Mr. Joe Thain after this investigation.
I do not want to prolong this discussion and feel I have explained as much as I can at this time. This work is progressing favourably. There were 500 men employed over the winter and it is expected that from 1,500 to

the first tunnel and found that the 25-foot hole has been extended 600 feet with the ring beams and cement. As I say, the work is progressing rapidly and on schedule, and it is expected that the job will be completed in 1965.

The payments that may be obtained under the act at the present time are too low and bear no reasonable relationship whatsoever to the cost of production. The government should consider a substantial increase in the payments under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. With crop production costs as they are at the present time, I think a very powerful argument could be made for doubling the payments under this act. That would be a very-I do not like to use this word-"conservative" payment; it would be a very low payment and in no way adequate to meet the farmers' cost of production. The government has another scheme which is closely related to this scheme, namely the crop insurance provision. We have had some very critical things to say about the crop insurance scheme. 90205-6-228
Question
The following answer, deposited with the Clerk of the house, is printed in the official report of debates pursuant to standing order 39:

1.	Have any of the alleged illegal entrants of Chinese origin been offered any amnesty or been provided with any facilities for regularizing their entry to Canada, and, if so, how many such entrants have been affected?
2.	Has the government, or any minister thereof, waived any provisions of the law in so far as the alleged illegal entrants are concerned, and, if so. which particular provisions have been so waived, in how many instances, and by authority of which particular provisions of which statute or regulation?
3.	Have any prosecutions been entered into with respect to the said illegal entry, and, if so, what charges were laid in each case, and what has been the disposition thereof?
Answer by: Hon. Ellen L. Fairclough (Minisier
of Citizenship and Immigration):
1.	The announcement made in the House of Commons on June 9, 1960, stated that "it is not the intention in connection with the current investigation to prosecute or deport from the country any Chinese presently in Canada, who have not themselves engaged in assisting other Chinese apart from their own relatives, to enter Canada illegally".
The announcement affects equally, on the basis of the terms and conditions set out therein, all illegal Chinese entrants to Canada who were in Canada at the time the announcement was made. It is not possible to state the total number involved, since the full number of those who have themselves entered illegally and of those who have helped their own relatives to enter is not yet known.
Facilities have been provided in each of the main immigration offices across Canada to assist individuals who wish to make a full disclosure of the circumstances of their illegal entry into Canada or of the help they have given to other illegal entrants. Special staff members have been trained and assigned for this purpose. Where it is satisfactorily established that full and complete disclosure has been made, each case is then studied to determine what further steps are required to regularize the status of the individual in Canada. In some cases correction of certain information on departmental records may be all that is required. In other cases where an individual has entered under a false identity,
or through use of a Canadian passport obtained by fraud, it may be necessary to recommend that permanent landing be granted by order in council under the individual's true identity. In other cases the individual may have acquired Canadian citizenship under a false identity, and this may have to be corrected.
2.	No provisions of the Immigration Act have been waived. Section 26 of the act provides that the director of immigration shall order an "inquiry" to be held, which may lead to a deportation order being issued, in cases where he has received a written report under section 19, and "where he considers that an inquiry is warranted". Since the announcement in the House of Commons on June 9, 1960, the director has exercised his discretion under section 26, and has not ordered an inquiry to be held in cases which appear to fall within the scope of the announcement.
3.	No prosecutions have been entered with respect to illegal entry, except in cases falling outside the scope of the announcement made in the House of Commons on June 9, 1960.
